# How an LLM writes, and structured outputs {#sec-ch06}

::: {.epigraph by="Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, 1922"}
The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.
:::

When ChatGPT answers, the words appear a few at a time, as if someone were typing. It isn't an animation. The model really doesn't know the end of its sentence when it writes the beginning. It picks one small piece, then the next, each time looking back at everything so far.

That one detail explains why long answers are slow, why the same question gets different answers, and why you pay per token. It also explains why "just ask the LLM" is an awkward way to make a decision.

::: {.goals}
- Describe the generation loop: predict, pick, append, repeat.
- Explain why answer length drives latency and cost, and why the same question can get different answers.
- Recognise how "just ask for JSON" fails, and what constrained decoding does and doesn't fix.
- Compare three kinds of confidence: stated in the text, read from token probabilities, and returned by a decision model.
:::

## One token at a time

An LLM reads **tokens**: chunks of text, often parts of words. Common words are one token; rare strings (hostnames, typos, codes) break into many, and you pay per token. A number like 0.87 may be split in ways that don't match its meaning, one reason LLMs are clumsy with arithmetic.

Every token comes from the same loop.

![The generation loop. The model reads everything so far, produces a probability for every possible next token, one gets picked, it's appended, and the loop runs again.](/figures/ch10/loop.pdf){#fig-loop-06}

Read everything so far. Produce a probability for every token in the vocabulary, often around a hundred thousand. Pick one. Append it. Repeat (@fig-loop-06).

The picking hides a choice. Always take the likeliest token (**greedy**: predictable but dull), or roll a die weighted by the probabilities (**sampling**: varied). **Temperature** sets how bold the die is: below 1, likely tokens win more; above 1, unlikely ones get a real chance.

## Length is time

Each token waits for the one before, so token fifty can't exist before token forty-nine. The length of the answer sets how long it takes.

![How long an answer takes under simple, illustrative assumptions: a short wait before the first token, then a steady stream. A one-word label is fast. An explanation takes seconds. Step-by-step reasoning takes tens of seconds.](/figures/ch10/latency.pdf){#fig-latency-06}

Assume {{< num ch10 ttft f2 >}} seconds before the first token and {{< num ch10 tps int >}} tokens a second after that (illustrative numbers, not measured). Then a one-word answer takes about {{< num ch10 lat_1 f1 >}} seconds. An explanation of a few hundred tokens takes about {{< num ch10 lat_300 f1 >}}. And 1,500 tokens of step-by-step reasoning take about {{< num ch10 lat_1500 int >}} (@fig-latency-06). "Reasoning" models write long chains of thought before answering: much better on hard problems, much slower, because every thinking token goes through the loop.

::: {.keyidea}
For a writing model, every word of the answer costs time and money, including the words you didn't need.
:::

## Same question, different answers

Ask the same question twice with sampling on and you may get two answers. Useful for a poem; a problem for deciding whether an alert is real. We asked the book's stand-in LLM (built to behave like typical LLMs, not a copy of any product) about forty borderline alerts, twenty times each.

![Forty borderline alerts, each asked the same question twenty times at temperature 0.7. The bar shows how often the answer was "malicious". All but one of them got different answers across the twenty runs.](/figures/ch10/variance.pdf){#fig-variance-06}

In @fig-variance-06, {{< num ch10 n_split int >}} of the {{< num ch10 n_alerts int >}} alerts flipped between answers. Set the temperature to zero and the answers repeat much more often. But the *uncertainty* doesn't go away. You just stop seeing it.

::: {.keyidea}
Sampling turns a model's uncertainty into randomness in its answers. Temperature zero hides it; it doesn't remove it.
:::

And nothing in the loop checks whether the sentence is *true*. The model produces a likely-sounding next token. It can write a fluent, confident, completely made-up hostname or citation, because that's the kind of thing that *would* come next. That's called **hallucination**.

## Asking for JSON

Software can't read a paragraph; it needs a field and a value. So every team connecting an LLM to software adds *"Reply only with JSON"* to the prompt. It works, almost always. "Almost" adds up. Over 4,000 alerts, {{< num ch11 prompt_fail_share pct1 >}} of the answers came back broken, wrapped in extra text, or with an extra field. At seven hundred alerts a day, that's about {{< num ch11 prompt_fail_per_day int >}} failures every day.

![What came back when we asked for JSON, over 4,000 alerts. With only the prompt, some responses were wrapped in friendly chat, some were cut off mid-object, and some were valid JSON with a field nobody asked for. With JSON mode on, the first two problems vanish. The third doesn't.](/figures/ch11/json-failures.pdf){#fig-json-failures}

Three failures (@fig-json-failures): chatty text around the JSON ("Sure! Here is..."), a response cut off mid-way, and valid JSON with an invented field, here an attacker's country that isn't in the alert. The last is the worst: it parses fine, so made-up data slips in unnoticed.

The loop offers a fix: at each step, forbid any token that would break the format. That's **constrained decoding**, sold as "JSON mode" or "structured outputs" [@willard2023]. It guarantees the *shape* of the answer.

::: {.keyidea}
Constrained decoding makes the answer parse. It doesn't make it right.
:::

It can still say "benign" for a real attack, in perfect syntax. Treat model output like text a stranger typed into a web form: parse it strictly, reject unknown fields, and if parsing fails, send the case to a person, never to an automatic action.

## Three confidences

Say the JSON is perfect: `"verdict": "malicious", "confidence": 0.95`. Can you put a threshold on that 0.95? There are three different numbers you might use:

- **The confidence the model wrote** is just text: the characters "0.95", picked like any other tokens.
- **The token probability** is the probability the model gave to "malicious" as the next token; many APIs return it.
- **A decision model's probability** comes from a model whose actual output is a probability for each option.

![Reliability of three "confidences" on the same test alerts, all reading the same raw text. The stated confidence barely separates attacks from harmless alerts. The token probability ranks well but is overconfident. The decision model ranks best and also sits close to the diagonal. Synthetic: the stand-ins reflect design choices, not measurements of real models.](/figures/ch11/three-confidences.pdf){#fig-three-confidences}

The stand-in wrote only {{< num ch11 n_distinct_stated int >}} different confidence values, {{< num ch11 share_stated_ge_09 pct >}} of them 0.9 or higher, a pattern many people see in real models too. Stated confidence ranks alerts poorly, with an AUC of {{< num ch11 verbal.auc f2 >}}. The token probability ranks much better ({{< num ch11 token.auc f2 >}}) but is overconfident (ECE {{< num ch11 token.ece f3 >}}). The decision model ranks slightly better again ({{< num ch11 jev_text.auc f2 >}}). It's also well calibrated, with an ECE of {{< num ch11 jev_text.ece f3 >}} (@fig-three-confidences).

Oddly, the stated confidence has the lowest ECE ({{< num ch11 verbal.ece f3 >}}). That isn't a win: saying nearly the same thing about every alert can be right *on average* while telling you nothing about which alert is which. Calibration and ranking: you need both. Studies of real models disagree on stated confidence [@tian2023; @xiong2024]; the only safe rule is to measure your own.

Why isn't a token's probability the answer's probability? Because the model is choosing among tens of thousands of tokens, not two answers. "malicious", "Malicious" and " malicious" are different tokens, and some probability goes to starting a sentence instead. You can add up the right tokens and rescale, but then you're hand-building a decision model on top of a writing model.

::: {.keyidea}
The probability of a token isn't the probability of an answer.
:::

## The typed alternative

So ask differently. Don't ask a writer for text shaped like a decision; ask a model whose natural output *is* the decision. Declare the question and its possible answers; get back data, with a probability for every option.

![The same question, two ways. On the left, an LLM writes JSON, including a confidence it wrote as text. On the right, a typed question returns data: a probability for a yes-or-no question, and one for every label of a choice.](/figures/ch11/typed-vs-text.pdf){#fig-typed-vs-text}

Jev's interface looks like this (@fig-typed-vs-text). There's nothing to parse and no format to break. The labels can only be the ones you listed. And the number is designed to be a probability, so it's a claim you can check. Part III looks at Jev in detail.

::: {.breaks}
Token probabilities describe the next piece of text, not the truth of the answer. JSON mode doesn't stop a model from choosing the wrong value, or from copying an attacker's text into a field. Strict checking doesn't catch a value that's valid but wrong: a threat-intel score misread as 0.18 instead of 0.81 passes every schema. Providers update their models, so "temperature 0" behaviour can change between versions. Fix the model version for anything you'll audit. And typed decision APIs have their own limits: they give probabilities without reasons, and their calibration still has to be tested on your data.
:::

::: {.threshold}
The team wants to auto-close alerts that the LLM labels "benign" with a stated confidence of at least 0.95. Would you trust that threshold? What would you put a threshold on instead?

(No. 0.95 and 0.99 are the model's favourite values, so the threshold filters almost nothing. Put the threshold on the best-calibrated probability you have, checked on recent history. Set its position by what mistakes cost, as Chapter 4 shows.)
:::

::: {.exercises}
1. Explain in your own words why generation can't be parallelised the way reading can.
2. Using the illustrative latency numbers, how long would 10,000 alerts take to label one at a time with a one-word answer? With a 300-token explanation?
:::
